papers.title_in_file: Quantum transport in randomized quantum graphs
papers.version_note: arXiv:2404.09106v2 (20 Dec 2024), published as APL Quantum 1, 046126 (2024).
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper that defines the transmission coefficient of randomized quantum graphs (quantum graphs with random edge removal) and studies it for complete graphs on n vertices minus one edge.

assertions.value: The authors study open quantum graphs built from the complete graph on n vertices with one edge removed, with two leads attached to the vertices of the removed edge as the entrance and exit channels, from which they calculate the transmission coefficient.
quotes: We consider the case of complete graphs on n vertices with an edge removed and attached to two leads to represent the entrance and exit channels, from where we calculate the transmission coefficient.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the paper's own setup.

assertions.value: The authors use the Gilbert G(n, p) random graph model, in which each pair of vertices is connected with probability p and not connected with probability q = (1 - p).
quotes: The second way to define
a random graph is given by associating a probability p to con-
nect each two vertices from n labeled vertices, and a proba-
bility q = (1 − p) to not have a connection between them
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the model used, Section II.B.

assertions.value: The authors use the stationary free Schrödinger operator on each edge with Neumann-Kirchhoff boundary conditions at the vertices, and add semi-infinite leads to the vertices to make an open quantum graph with c scattering channels.
quotes: we consider the stationary free Schrödinger operator H = −(ℏ2/2m)d2/dx2 on each edge, and use Neumann-Kirchhoff boundary conditions on the corresponding vertices47,48.
leads (semi-infinite edges) to its vertices
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own model in Section II.C.

assertions.value: The paper states that for Neumann-Kirchhoff boundary conditions the individual vertex amplitudes are independent of k, with ri = (2/di) - 1 and ti = 2/di, where di is the degree of vertex i.
quotes: For Neumann-Kirchhoff boundary conditions, these individual quantum amplitudes are independent of k, and are explicitly given by ri = (2/di) − 1 and ti = 2/di, where di is degree of the vertex i.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as part of the paper's own model in Section II.C.

assertions.value: Definition III.1 defines the exact transmission coefficient of a randomized quantum graph as the sum over all quantum subgraphs that span the original graph of p to the power of the subgraph's edge count, times one minus p to the power of the number of removed edges, times the squared modulus of the subgraph's scattering amplitude, where p is the randomization parameter.
assertions.anchor: Definition III.1, Eq. (6), Section III, p.3
quotes: Definition III.1 (Exact transmission coefficient of a RQG). Let ΓGc be a quantum graph with c scattering channels.
in which p is the randomization parameter associated with the probability of the existence of an edge of the original quantum graph.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition III.1 in Section III.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a complete quantum graph on n vertices the number of quantum subgraphs is a power of two in the number of edges (the exponent is printed flat in the text layer), that the count scales exponentially with the number of vertices, and that applying the exact definition can be hard to implement.
quotes: Thus, the number of subgraphs scales exponentially with the number of vertices and the application of Eq.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the cost limit of its exact definition in Section III.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the exponent as 2(2n); the exact form is not recoverable from the quote.

assertions.value: The authors propose a Monte Carlo method: for each number of edges they draw an ensemble of subgraphs with exactly that number of edges, uniformly at random, without repetition and counting isomorphic subgraphs separately, and average the squared scattering amplitude over the ensemble.
quotes: we propose a Monte Carlo method for calculating the scatter-

The subgraphs of the ensemble are chosen uniformly and randomly among all the possible subgraphs ΓcF having exactly |EΓcF | edges, without repetition and taking into account all the isomorphic subgraphs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own procedure in Section III.

assertions.value: The authors state they sample without identifying isomorphic subgraphs because determining whether two subgraphs are isomorphic is a hard problem.
quotes: as determining whether two subgraphs are isomorphic is a hard problem56.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement the paper attributes to reference 56.

assertions.value: Proposition 1 states that the approximated transmission coefficient of a randomized quantum graph is the sum over edge counts of the binomial coefficient times p to the edge count times one minus p to the removed-edge count times the ensemble-average squared scattering amplitude, and that as the ensembles grow larger it converges closer to the exact coefficient.

As the ensembles grow larger, TR((fΓ,iGc) )(k, p) converges even
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is only partly quotable because the text layer scrambles the formula and conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: The appendix argument sets the ensemble size equal to the full set of subgraphs and so shows equality only in that limit; it gives no convergence rate.

(8) and taking the limit in which each ensemble becomes the set of all subgraphs with a given number of edges, so that the double sum becomes the sum over all spanning subgraphs, which equals the exact transmission coefficient.

assertions.certainty_reason: The proof's limit step is not quotable because the text layer scrambles it.
assertions.reader_inference: The proof is the limit of full enumeration, so it shows consistency, not accuracy at finite ensemble size.

assertions.value: For the complete graph on four vertices minus an edge the authors compute the exact transmission by evaluating all its quantum subgraphs, identifying 14 nonisomorphic quantum subgraphs and their numbers of isomorphisms and transmission amplitudes (Table I).
assertions.anchor: Section IV, Table I, Eq. (9), p.4-5
quotes: we can calculate the exact transmission for the randomized quantum graph R(Γ2K4e ) by evaluating the scattering transmission for all its quantum subgraphs, Eq. (6).
The individual results are shown in Table I, where we identified 14 nonisomorphic quantum subgraphs and evaluated their number of isomorphisms and transmission amplitudes.
assertions.certainty_reason: A computed result from one study.

assertions.value: For the graph on 6 vertices minus an edge, with 16384 possible subgraphs, the authors report that the exact transmission coefficient and the Monte Carlo approximation with ensembles of up to 250 subgraphs are almost indistinguishable, with a maximum error of 2.3%.
quotes: For K6e, there are 214 = 16384 possible subgraphs, which must be considered for the exact calculation.
the results are almost indistinguishable from the approximated one, displaying a maximum error of 2.3%. This is an indication that our method is adequate.
ensembles with the same number of edges with up to 250 quantum subgraphs
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one graph.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper tests the approximation on n = 6 only, where the exact answer is computable; accuracy at larger n is not measured against an exact result.

assertions.value: The authors report for the studied ensembles that the transmission is periodic in k times edge length, so they use the interval from 0 to 2 pi; that it vanishes for all k times edge length when the subgraph has 1 edge or fewer; and that for exactly 2 edges the signal is either fully transmitted or not transmitted at all.
quotes: i) the transmission is periodic, so we concentrate on the interval 0 ≤ kℓ ≤ 2π; ii) the transmission vanishes for all kℓ when the number of edges |EΓ2F | is less than or equal to 1
iii) for |EΓ2F | = 2, due to the Neumann-Kirchhoff boundary conditions, either the signal is fully transmitted or there is no transmission at all
assertions.certainty_reason: Observations from computed ensembles, stated without a proof.

assertions.value: The authors report that at k times edge length equal to pi the subgraph ensembles transmit only for 2 to 9 edges, and that the transmission shows a band of full suppression around that value even when up to 4 edges are removed, which they attribute to destructive interference and take to suggest the graph can still act as a filter under edge removal.
quotes: iv) for kℓ = π, we notice that there is transmission only in the interval of 2 ≤ |EΓ2F | ≤ 9
v) the transmission probability displays a band of full suppression in the region around kℓ = π, even when one removes up to 4 edges due to destructive interference in the transmission.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one graph family.
assertions.reader_inference: The filter use is the authors' suggestion; no filter is built or tested.

assertions.value: The authors report that at k times edge length equal to pi the subgraph transmissions they evaluated were either 0 or 1.
quotes: we noticed that the values obtained at kℓ = π were either 0 or 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical observation, not proved.

assertions.value: The authors report that the transmission is not monotonic in p, so a value pm of the randomization parameter exists at which the transmission is maximal and larger than at p = 1.0, meaning randomized quantum graphs can transmit more than the deterministic graph at some values of k times edge length.
quotes: We can also observe in Figs. 8 and 10 that the transmission is not monotonic as a function of p, then it is possible to find the value of the randomization parameter, pm, in which the transmission is maximum and larger than the transmission for p = 1.0.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result for n = 6, 7 and 8 at two values of k times edge length.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper tests two values of k times edge length only.

assertions.value: The authors tabulate, at k times edge length equal to pi/8, pm of 0.458, 0.365 and 0.305 with maximal transmission 0.436, 0.358 and 0.307 for n = 6, 7 and 8; at pi, pm of 0.334, 0.271 and 0.233 with maximal transmission 0.259, 0.239 and 0.223.
assertions.certainty_reason: Computed values from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the maximum value of the transmission is shifted to the left as the number of vertices increases, and in the conclusions that the maximum value of the transmission decreases as n increases.
assertions.anchor: Section IV p.6; Section V p.7
quotes: The results show that the maximum value of the transmission is shifted to the left as we increase the number of vertices.
with the corresponding maximum value of the transmission decreasing as one increases n.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result for n = 6, 7, 8.

assertions.value: The authors state, without a test beyond the one graph checked against an exact result, that the methodology will give even better results when the number of edges in the quantum graph increases.
quotes: our methodology will give even better results when one increases the number of edges in the quantum graph.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the exact-versus-approximate comparison is shown only for n = 6.
assertions.reader_inference: No exact result is computed for n = 7 or 8, so this is untested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that imperfections include damping, leakage and noise, and that they concentrate only on simple quantum graphs with random edges, which does not cover the many possibilities.
quotes: Here, however, we shall concentrate on the case of simple quantum graphs with random edges. This does not cover the many possibilities
assertions.certainty_reason: The introduction states the scope of the study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the definition also lets one randomize a chosen set of edges instead of all edges, and that other generalizations will be reported in future works.
quotes: The way the randomization of quantum graphs is defined here also allows us to randomize a given set of edges of the graph instead of all edges of the graph
These and other generalizations will be reported in future works.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this as open work in Section V.
